question: The changing security landscape in Europe requires an efficient and resilient infrastructure for military mobility. Northern Germany serves as a central logistics hub for the deployment of troops and equipment to Eastern Europe. Ports, waterways and their hinterland connections play a key role in ensuring security of supply, economic stability and military operational capability.
At the same time, significant shortcomings remain in approval procedures, infrastructure resilience and cross-border operational coordination. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the capacity of transport and port infrastructure in northern Germany in terms of its suitability for military mobility?

What specific regulatory and operational measures does the Commission plan to implement as part of the military mobility package to remove existing obstacles – such as lengthy approval procedures, inconsistent national rules and regulations and infrastructural constraints – quickly and effectively?

To what extent does the Commission intend to specifically prioritise and provide financial support for infrastructure projects in northern Germany that are highly relevant in terms of their dual-use nature, and on the basis of which criteria does it ensure that these investments contribute directly to strengthening military mobility and resilience?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Commission, supported by the EU Military Staff and working with Member States, is reviewing transport infrastructure against military needs to identify key chokepoints. This work focuses on the four priority military mobility corridors set out in the Council’s Military Requirements, with the aim of building a resilient and operational network.

Northern Germany remains a key EU military mobility hub, including its port infrastructure. The EU Military Mobility Package1, adopted in November 2025, tackles barriers in regulation, infrastructure and capabilities.

It simplifies rules and procedures, introduces a new emergency framework, promotes pooling and sharing of capabilities, advances digitalisation, supports the readiness of dual-use infrastructure, and strengthens governance and coordination.

Together, these measures support the creation of an EU-wide Military Mobility Area2 by 2027, paving the way to a ‘Military Schengen’, enabling large-scale military transport of troops and equipment at speed and scale. Financial support for projects with a multinational defence dimension may be provided through the Security Action for Europe programme.

For dual-use projects, funding may also be available from several instruments, in particular the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF), National and Regional Partnership Plans, and cohesion policy funds. Under the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), EUR 1.69 billion has been allocated to 95 dual-use projects under CEF.

For the next MFF, the Commission proposes increasing the CEF military mobility budget tenfold to EUR 17.65 billion. The European Investment Bank’s new defence lending policy can also support such projects through loans and guarantees.
